newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Embattled Coles in profit slump.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Coles in profit slump.

text.p: Australia's largest retailer, Coles Myer Ltd, on Tuesday announced a 34 percent drop in annual net profit, admitting the performance was disappointing but rejecting suggestions the embattled group should be broken up.

The group's A$280.4 million (US$221.5 million) profit for the year to July 28 followed a record result of A$423.4 million in 1994/95, but Coles Myer said two of its biggest earners were performing poorly and could not be turned around quickly.
"Getting Coles Myer moving is like trying to wheel-spin a steam-roller. It doesn't happen easily," chief executive Peter Bartels told a news conference in Melbourne.

Coles, which accounts for almost 18 cents of every retail dollar spent in Australia, said steep profit slumps in its Kmart discount chain and Myer Grace Bros department stores were the most disappointing aspects of the result.

Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) from Kmart more than halved in 1995/96 and Myer Grace Bros' EBIT fell 27 percent, dragging total retail EBIT down 14.8 percent to A$535 million despite an eight percent rise in overall sales revenue.

Coles' bottom line, which included a net abnormal loss of A$31.5 million stemming from its troubled toy retail unit, was roughly in line with expectations. Coles shares closed just two cents lower at A$4.57 on Tuesday.

"We are disappointed to some degree with our result. We would have liked it to have been better...but the market has been very tough," Bartels said. He added the group planned to dispose of up to A$1.3 billion in property assets in 1996/97.
"At the retail line, I think we performed well with the exception of Kmart and Myer Grace Bros."

Once a blue-chip favourite, Coles Myer has suffered a string of recent management woes, including a bitter boardroom feud which led major shareholder Solomon Lew to resign as executive chairman last year and a controversy over corporate governance.

Australia's financial press has also speculated that New Zealand corporate raider Brierley Investments Ltd is circling the retailer's share register after building up a seven percent stake. Commentators have also suggested a break-up of the group's vast retailing empire to realise its true potential.
Bartels, who replaced Lew at the helm, denied management was distracted by these events and rejected suggestions that Coles Myer would deliver improved shareholder value if broken up.
He said profits needed to be ploughed back into store refurbishments aimed at better targeting customers.

Coles' chief retail executive, Dennis Eck, agreed, telling Reuters the group expected to post higher profits in the current 1996/97 year as the group returned to its traditional retailing strengths and rebuilt close ties with suppliers.
"Business by business I expect improvement," Eck said.
Some stock analysts said on Tuesday the result actually came in slightly above expectations. They said they were likely to make minor upgrades to their 1996/97 profit forecasts for Coles.

"I have upgraded my estimates a little bit. They're getting some good growth in supermarkets, addressing problems in (toy retailer) World 4 Kids and Kmart...though it's going to be a slow recovery," a Melbourne-based analyst told Reuters.
